Sharon Claydon The question is that the amendments moved by the member for Kooyong be agreed to. Anika Wells I thank the member for Kooyong for moving these amendments. The government will not support the amendments. We do not support imposing new reporting obligations through this bill. These amendments would create a new regulatory reporting regime for sporting, cultural and recreational organisations with annual turnover above $50 million requiring disclosure of gambling related revenue and publication by ACMA. This proposal is outside the scope of the bill's aim to directly reduce harm from gambling and would impose additional compliance and administrative burdens without a demonstrated impact. The government agrees that more must be done to stop gambling advertising from proliferating online. The restrictions introduced by the government ban wagering advertising online by default, unless online content services implement the triple lock requirements—that is, users must be over 18 years of age, logged into an account and have not opted out of wagering advertising. The government takes seriously our responsibility to protect Australians, particularly children and young people, from the harms of online gambling. The government has supported an amendment to establish a wagering advertising opt out register to provide individuals with a one stop shop to opt out of receiving all wagering advertising content. We have worked constructively with the opposition and the crossbench to consider practical amendments to this bill, and I'd like to thank my shadow counterpart, Senator Henderson, in the other place for working with me diligently over a number of weeks in order to get this ready for consideration today in the House. I thank you for your conscientious work, Senator Henderson, and I thank the House. Question negatived. Long debate text truncated.

Moved the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026, saying the BetStop review found limited public awareness and that gambling companies should fund promotion rather than taxpayers. Proposed expanding cost recovery to cover ACMA and departmental activities supporting the register, including awareness raising; debate was adjourned.

Moved that the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026 be referred to the Standing Committee on Social Policy and Legal Affairs for an advisory report by 11 August 2026. Argued that the bill fell short of the Murphy report, lacked adequate consultation and required evidence-based scrutiny of advertising restrictions and protections; the motion was seconded and the question was put.

Moved the second reading of the Interactive Gambling Amendment (Gambling Reform) Bill 2026 and two companion cost-recovery bills, agreed with the Coalition and Senator Henderson, that would restrict wagering advertising during children's programming and live sport, require a triple-lock age-verification and opt-out system, create a Wagering Advertising Opt-out Register funded by a levy on wagering providers, ban inducement marketing to vulnerable customers and BetStop deregistrants, and prohibit online keno and foreign-matched lotteries, noting a February 2026 statutory review found only one in four Australians know BetStop exists; a Coalition senator welcomed the amendments strengthening protections while criticising the original bill and the government's handling of the reforms.
This bill strengthens how the social media minimum age framework is enforced.
It expands the eSafety Commissioner's powers to demand documents and information from anyone relevant to compliance checks.
Civil penalties for breaking minimum age rules would double to 60,000 penalty units, worth about $99 million for a body corporate.
Expands the eSafety Commissioner's information-gathering powers to compel production of documents from any person.
Doubles the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 2, Part 4A from 30,000 to 60,000 penalty units.
Increases the maximum civil penalty for contraventions of Division 4, Part 4A from 500 to 1,000 penalty units.
Providers of age-restricted social media platforms and the eSafety Commissioner are affected.

But the truth is that, in the modern age, if you want to share and communicate with your constituency, or if you're in business and you want to share and communicate with customers, if you're not on a digital platform then you're missing out. Alison Penfold Fuel security is economic security and fuel security is national security. Recent events have exposed how vulnerable Australia remains. We are one of the world's great energy producing nations, yet we remain heavily dependent on imported liquid fuels. We've allowed refining capacity to decline, and we've failed to build sufficient storage capacity. We continue to rely on international supply chains for a resource that underpins almost every aspect of modern life. No fuel means no freight and no food, and no food means empty shelves. Regional Australia sits at the front line of that vulnerability. The lesson from this crisis is clear. Australia needs more than temporary tax relief. Australia needs a long-term fuel security strategy. We need stronger fuel reserves. We need greater storage capacity. We need stronger sovereign capability, and we need more resilient supply chains. We need governments willing to think beyond the next headline and beyond the next election cycle. What Australians want is not another temporary fix. They want a government that understands what is happening to their country, and, increasingly, Australians are concluding that this government does not, because, after four years of the Albanese Labor government, Australians are paying more for almost everything and getting less in return. There are higher power bills, higher grocery bills, higher fuel bills, higher insurance costs, higher housing costs and higher taxes. This government likes to blame global events for Australia's problems. It blames wars. It blames supply chains. It blames international markets. But Australians know better. The cost-of-living crisis did not begin in the Middle East. The housing crisis did not begin in the Middle East. The energy crisis did not begin in the Middle East. Michael McCormack The Housing Industry Association's executive director for compliance and workplace relations, Stuart Collins, has some advice for this Labor government. He said: This bill— the Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026— is being sold as a modest administrative tidy-up of the Fair Work Commission. Asked how proposed workplace relations legislation could prevent corruption and protect value for money given concerns about enterprise agreements and the CFMEU; the minister said the bill would allow, but not require, preference for genuinely negotiated agreements and announced consultation on a construction code for Commonwealth procurement.

Opposed the Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026's procurement provisions, supporting its Fair Work Commission measures on artificial intelligence but arguing union-preference rules could disadvantage small businesses, reduce value for money and repeat problems associated with Queensland's former scheme and alleged CFMEU corruption; the debate was then interrupted.

Moved to suspend standing orders and give precedence to a coalition bill addressing the Fair Work Commission backlog, arguing that the government's bill combined those reforms with procurement, grants, and contracting preferences for businesses linked to union agreements; later moved that the question be put.

Spoke on the Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026, supporting reforms to address the Fair Work Commission's workload but opposing provisions that would allow procurement preferences for businesses with union-backed enterprise agreements, arguing they create corruption risks and require separate scrutiny.

Considered the Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Bill 2026 and put opposition, Australian Greens, and Senator David Pocock amendments concerning workplace determinations, less favourable terms, flexibility and consultation provisions, retrospective variations, and a proposed inquiry into corruption risks in Commonwealth procurement and grants before the bill's remaining stages were agreed to.

Argued that allowing Commonwealth supply-chain preferences for businesses with union-backed enterprise agreements could discriminate against comparable businesses. Called for an inquiry into alleged corruption and organised crime involving the construction sector and the CFMEU, stating that failed inquiries had left serious concerns unresolved and that corruption could add 15 to 30 per cent to infrastructure costs.
Workplace Relations Legislation Amendment (Building Cooperative Workplaces No. 1) Act 2026

Moved the Electoral Legislation Amendment (Electoral Communications) Bill 2025, calling for guardrails against misleading political advertising, including AI-generated deepfakes, to be enacted before the next election; a seconder supported prohibiting materially misleading factual content while preserving political opinions, and debate was adjourned.

The member moved amendments to the Family Law Amendment Bill 2023 requiring a reasonable attempt to consult on long‑term decisions, codifying the *Rice v Asplund* test for reopening final parenting orders before any hearing, and requiring a reasonable attempt to understand obligations as a defence to contravention. Further amendments sought to include family violence history and family violence orders as mandatory considerations, define repeated legal systems abuse as family violence, and add cultural‑linguistic background factors for children’s best interests. The government did not support the amendments, noting the bill would be referred to a committee.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Consumer Data Right) Bill 2022

The Treasury Laws Amendment (Consumer Data Right) Bill 2022 was supported across the chamber, expanding consumers’ ability to direct accredited parties to take actions such as switching providers or updating personal details. Coalition speakers called for a Senate committee inquiry and a dedicated minister for the digital economy, while Labor criticised the previous government’s record on digital infrastructure and noted the scheme had been left unfunded.
Aged Care Amendment (Implementing Care Reform) Bill 2022

The speech welcomed the Aged Care Amendment (Implementing Care Reform) Bill 2022 and urged the government to accelerate implementing all 140 recommendations of the royal commission into aged care. It supported mandatory 24/7 registered nurses in facilities but raised concerns about exemption criteria, delegated legislation, the $460 million cost over forward estimates, and a shortfall of 850 nurses to meet the bill's requirements.
Fair Work Amendment (Paid Family and Domestic Violence Leave) Bill 2022

The speaker welcomed the 10 days paid domestic violence leave bill as a good first step but argued it is insufficient, calling for expanded leave, nationally consistent definitions of non-physical abuse, better resourcing of support services, and action on the $13.6 billion annual economic cost of domestic violence. They noted 427 domestic violence assaults and 229 breached AVOs in their electorate of Warringah over one year.

The speaker supported the Jobs and Skills Australia Bill 2022, which establishes a statutory body to replace the National Skills Commissioner and provide independent advice on workforce skills and training needs, including research into emerging industries like clean energy. The speaker also called for increased women's workforce participation through affordable childcare and expanded parental leave, and urged the inclusion of universities in the bill's consultation requirements.
Treasury Laws Amendment (Electric Car Discount) Bill 2022

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Electric Car Discount) Bill is a small, welcome step but far too timid, calling on the government to instead pursue far bolder policies including fuel efficiency standards, universal charging infrastructure, and a more ambitious emissions target than 43% by 2030. They noted that transport accounts for 17% of Australia’s carbon footprint and that if just 10% of light vehicles provided vehicle‑to‑grid power, it could supply nearly three times the overnight capacity of Snowy 2.0.

The speaker welcomed the Climate Change Bill 2022 as progress but argued it is not comprehensive, lacking mechanisms, risk assessments, adaptation plans, and a ratchet mechanism, and criticised the 43% emissions reduction target by 2030 as politically rather than scientifically motivated, urging greater ambition and no new fossil fuel projects.
